2027 NOAA FISHERIES–ALASKA DEPARTMENT OF FISH AND GAME SOUTHEAST ALASKA PINK SALMON HARVEST FORECAST

The 2027 Southeast Alaska pink salmon harvest is expected to be excellent, with a harvest forecast of 67 million fish. Juvenile pink salmon abundance measured in northern inside waters during summer 2026 was well above average, which suggests a large number of adults will be returning in 2027. Although salmon runs can vary due to changing ocean conditions, this forecast reflects the best available information from long-term National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Alaska Fisheries Science Center, Auke Bay Laboratories and Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) monitoring programs. The commercial purse seine fishery will be managed inseason based on aerial surveys and fishery performance indicators.

Forecast Methods

NOAA initiated the Southeast Alaska Coastal Monitoring (SECM) project in 1997 to better understand the effects of climate and nearshore ocean conditions on year-class strength of salmon and other ecologically related species (Orsi et al. 2000). Since 2018, the SECM project has been conducted cooperatively by NOAA and ADF&G using the ADF&G research vessel (R/V) Medeia, and the two agencies have combined efforts to produce a joint pink salmon harvest forecast using SECM data (Piston et al. 2019). The partnership between agencies facilitates the SECM survey and provides a wide variety of valuable information on the marine environment and juvenile salmon in northern Southeast Alaska (SEAK).

The 2027 SEAK pink salmon harvest forecast (Figures 1 and 2) is primarily based on juvenile pink salmon abundance indices collected by the SECM project in northern SEAK inside waters (Piston et al. 2026). These data were obtained from annual systematic surface trawl surveys conducted in June and July in upper Chatham and Icy Straits. Survey catches of juvenile pink salmon have been shown to be highly correlated with the harvest of adult pink salmon in the following year (Wertheimer et al. 2011). The juvenile abundance index is the higher of the June and July mean vesselcalibrated catch per unit effort (CPUE), with each monthly mean calculated from two standardized surface trawls at each of eight fixed sampling stations. The 2026 juvenile pink salmon abundance index of 3.51 is the highest for the time period the R/V Medeia has conducted the survey (2018–2025; mean 1.37; range 0.87–2.15) and is above the mean for even-year juvenile CPUE indices (1997–2024; mean 3.08; range 1.17–5.62).

The 2027 pink salmon forecast uses a method initially described by Wertheimer et al. (2006) and then later adapted by Orsi et al. (2016), Murphy et al. (2019), and Miller et al. (2022) and assumes a log-normal error structure and is based on multiple regression. The forecast models investigated included unadjusted or vessel-adjusted juvenile pink salmon CPUE; temperature data from SECM or satellite sea surface temperature data (Haung et al. 2017); a vessel factor; and an odd and even year factor. A total of 54 models were evaluated based on the one-step ahead mean absolute percent error for the last five years, while Akaike Information Criterion corrected for small sample sizes values were calculated to examine overparameterization, and adjusted R-squared values, significant terms, and overall p-values of the models were used to determine model fit.

2027 Pink Salmon Forecast

October 28, 2026

2027 Pink Salmon Forecast

October 28, 2026

The recommended model included the vessel-adjusted juvenile pink salmon CPUE, an odd and even year factor, and the mean satellite sea surface temperature data from northern SEAK from April, May, and June. Based on this model, the 2027 forecast point estimate of 67 million fish (80% prediction interval = 42 to 98 million) falls well into the excellent pink salmon harvest category. The categorical ranges of pink salmon harvest in SEAK were formulated from the 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles of historical harvest over the 66-year period 1960–2025:

Category Poor Weak Average Strong Excellent

Forecast Discussion

Range (millions) Less than 11 ≥11 to 19 ≥19 to 32 ≥32 to 48 Greater than or equal to 48

Percentile Less than 20th ≥20th to 40th ≥40th to 60th ≥60th to 80th Greater than or equal to 80th

The 2027 harvest forecast of 67 million pink salmon would be the largest harvest since 2013 (94.7 million) and would be the 4th highest harvest on record. This forecast reflects a 2026 juvenile pink salmon abundance index value (3.51) that was the largest since 2016 (8th highest of 30 years), and cool spring and early summer temperatures. Pink salmon harvests associated with juvenile indices above 3.00 have ranged from 35 to 95 million fish (mean = 59 million fish).

We continue to evaluate different treatments in our forecast model. Since 2004, 12 unique models have been used to produce the 24 harvest forecasts with changes occurring as additional information becomes available, and in response to poor predictive performance. For the 2027 harvest forecast, we again implemented an odd and even year factor to help address concerns that arose from underforecasting the 2021 and 2023 odd-year harvests. The extensive time series of SECM data extending from 1997 to present is now large enough to examine odd and even years separately which may better represent the segregated brood lines (oddand even-year) of pink salmon. In addition, due to concerns that slower trawl speed on the R/V Medeia was responsible for underforecasting the last two big, odd year harvests, we modified the trawl doors for the 2026 survey by increasing the trawl door weight. The additional weight allowed us to gain approximately 0.5 knots of speed while trawling and likely increased catches in 2026, although it is worth noting that average trawl speed was still below that of the R/V Northwest Explorer (conducted survey 2010–2017). Until we use the modified trawl doors for several years, we have no way to account for the potential change in catch rates, though we are still trawling within the speed range of other vessels that have been used on the survey and the wide prediction intervals of the forecast should capture the additional uncertainty this creates in the forecast. The fact that the survey caught above average numbers of pink salmon in nearly every trawl across a wide geographic range gives us confidence that pink salmon abundance is very high and the 2027 run will be in the excellent category.

While uncertainties are inherent in salmon forecasts, the NOAA/ADF&G joint pink salmon harvest forecast has maintained a strong track record (Figure 2), despite the unique challenges associated with pink salmon forecasting (Haeseker et al. 2005). As always, for the 2027 season, the department will manage the commercial purse seine fisheries inseason with aerial escapement surveys and fishery performance indicators.

2026 FALL DIRECTED DEMERSAL SHELF ROCKFISH FISHERY

The fall directed commercial fishery for demersal shelf rockfish (DSR) will open in portions of the Northern Southeast Inside (NSEI) and Southern Southeast Inside (SSEI) Subdistricts at 9:00 a.m., Tuesday, December 8, 2026. These areas will remain open until the fishery quotas are taken or until 4:00 p.m., Thursday, December 31, 2026, whichever occurs first. The DSR assemblage includes yelloweye, quillback, canary, copper, China, tiger, and rosethorn rockfish.

Directed DSR Commercial Fishery Harvest Guidelines

Groundfish Management Area Northern Southeast Inside (NSEI) Subdistrict Southern Southeast Inside (SSEI) Subdistrict

The 2026 annual directed commercial DSR harvest limit for the NSEI and SSEI Subdistricts is 55,000 round lb in each management area [5 AAC 28.160 (c)(2)]. Harvest from the directed DSR winter fishery in each area is deducted from the annual harvest limit, with the remaining amount available for harvest during the fall fishery. Because winter fishery harvest information is confidential in both areas, the remaining harvest limits are also confidential. Although the harvest amounts cannot be reported because fewer than three permits were fished, total harvest in each area remains below the annual limit of 55,000 round lb.

The directed DSR fishery catches will be closely monitored, and fishers are advised that area closures may occur on short notice. Closure notices will be announced by ADF&G advisory announcement, United States Coast Guard broadcast, National Weather Service broadcast, and the Groundfish Project’s telephone hotline 907-747-4882.

DSR Trip Limits (5 AAC 28.171) Directed DSR fishery trip limit regulations prohibit the take, possession, or delivery of DSR in excess of the trip limit amount. In the Southeast District east of 137° W long, a vessel or CFEC permit holder may not take or possess on board the vessel or deliver more than 6,000 lb of DSR (whole or bled weight) in any five-day period [5 AAC 28.171(d)]. When a vessel or CFEC permit holder delivers a 6,000 lb DSR trip limit, the fisher must wait five days from the day of their last possession of fish aboard the vessel, take of fish, or delivery, before taking any additional fish. All DSR taken in excess of 6,000 lb by a vessel or CFEC permit holder in any five-day period must be weighed and reported on an ADF&G fish ticket as a trip limit overage. All proceeds from the sale of DSR in excess of 6,000 lb shall be surrendered to the State of Alaska.

Permit and Registration (5 AAC 28.106) A Commercial Fisheries Entry Commission (CFEC) “Y” interim use permit is required for the directed DSR fishery and is issued specific to a gear type. This card must be obtained before registering and fishing. Fishers are required to register their vessel with the department prior to participating in the directed DSR fishery [5 AAC 28.106 (d)].

Logbooks (5 AAC 28.175) The operator of a vessel fishing in the directed DSR fishery is required to maintain an accurate logbook of all fishing operations (5 AAC 28.175). A copy of the logbook pages detailing a landing must be attached to the fish ticket documenting the landing. Logbooks for longline gear must include vessel and CFEC permit holder information, trip details (e.g., dates, port, crew size, bait, gear specifications), and set data such as gear deployment and retrieval times, start and end coordinates

Fall Directed DSR Fishery

October 22, 2026

(latitude and longitude in degrees and decimal minutes), gear amounts, and depth. They must also include the number or weight of all retained and released target and bycatch species, as well as any tag numbers from tagged fish [5 AAC 28.175(b)(1)]. Logbooks for dinglebar troll gear, mechanical jigging machines, or hand troll gear must include the date, the specific location of harvest by latitude and longitude, in degrees and decimal minutes, and nearest headland, the number of lines and total number of hooks used, the average depth fished, the hours fished, and the number of bycatch fish taken, by species, for each unique geographic location fished. For the target species, the number retained and the number discarded is required [5 AAC 28.175(b)(2)]. Logbooks are available at local ADF&G offices.

Legal Gear (5 AAC 28.130) In the Southeast District, DSR may be taken in the directed fishery by longline, hand troll, dinglebar troll, and mechanical jigging machines [5 AAC 28.130 (d)(3)(B)]. Dinglebar troll gear consists of a train made from a single line to which one or more leaders, lures, or baited hooks are attached, that is fastened to a single troll wire, and that is deployed and retrieved with a single power troll gurdy or a single hand troll gurdy with a terminally attached weight pulled through the water while a vessel is making way; only one operational unit of dinglebar troll gear may be onboard a vessel or deployed from the vessel at or below the surface of the water at a time; weights, including dinglebars, cannon balls, and other fishing weights, must be disconnected from the troll wires of all other gurdies that are mounted on the vessel: additional trains may not be trailed behind the vessel [5 AAC 28.130(h)(1)]. No more than five mechanical jigging machines may be operated from a vessel and no more than 30 hooks per line may be operated from a jigging machine. A mechanical jigging machine may not be deployed while the vessel is making way under mechanized propulsion and may not be anchored to the seafloor or operated unattached from the vessel [5 AAC 28.130 (h)(2)].

Vessels fishing for or transporting groundfish taken with dinglebar troll gear must display the letter “D” and vessels fishing for or transporting groundfish taken with mechanical jigging machines must display the letter “M” (5 AAC 28.135). A person may not operate a vessel that is displaying more than one of these letters at any time. A vessel may not display either letter while the vessel is being used to fish for salmon.

Closed Waters (5 AAC 28.150) Demersal shelf rockfish may not be taken in a directed fishery in the following waters (Figure 1):

(1) In the Ketchikan vicinity: all waters of Behm Canal, Clarence Strait, Tongass Narrows, Nichols Passage, George Inlet, Carroll Inlet, Thorne Arm, Revillagigedo Channel, and all contiguous waters enclosed by the latitude of Bushy Point Light, a line from Point Alava to the southernmost tip of Ham Island, a line from Cedar Point to Dall Head, and a line from Dall Head to a point in midstream Clarence Strait at the latitude of Dall Head to Caamano Point. (2) In the vicinity of Craig and Klawock: all waters of Ulloa Channel north of the latitude of Waterfall Cannery, and all waters enclosed by a line from the southernmost tip of St. Philip Island to the northernmost tip of San Fernando Island, to Point Cangrejo.

(3) In NSEI: the waters of Glacier Bay north of a line from Point Carolus at 58°22.694′ N. lat., 136°02.535′ W. long., to Point Gustavus at 58°22.748′ N. lat., 135°54.927′ W. long., and the waters of Dundas Bay north and west of a line running from 58°22.900′ N. lat., 136°25.300′ W. long., and 58°23.600′ N. lat., 136°24.600′ W. long.

Annette Islands Reserve The Annette Islands Reserve is a federally recognized Indian reservation in Alaska. The waters within 3,000 feet of Annette Island, Ham Island, Hemlock Island, Spire Island, Walker Island, Lewis Island, and the adjacent rocks and islets are designated within the fishing reserve (Figure 1). Fisheries within the reserve are managed by the Metlakatla Indian Community for authorized fisheries participants.

Groundfish Bycatch Allowances CFEC permit holders directed fishing for DSR must retain, weigh, and report all rockfish caught including thornyhead rockfish. All rockfish in excess of allowable bycatch limits shall be reported as bycatch overage on an ADF&G fish ticket. All proceeds from the sale of excess rockfish bycatch from state waters must be forfeited to the State of Alaska [5 AAC 28.171(a)].

Bycatch of species that do not fall under full retention requirements and are caught in excess of the allowable bycatch limit for a management area are required to be released at sea; bycatch retained in excess of the allowable bycatch limit must be forfeited to the State of Alaska and are subject to enforcement action. Task force meetings have rotated between communities to provide increased access and participation. Kuskokwim River Salmon Fishery Announcement #6

Emergency Order #3-S-WR-05-26

This is an announcement from the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) in Bethel for subsistence fishermen in the Kuskokwim River drainage.

As of August 19th, cumulative coho salmon passage at the Kuskokwim River sonar is approximately 156,000 fish, which is below the average passage of approximately 233,000 fish for this date. As of August 16th, approximately 112 coho salmon have been counted at the Kogrukluk weir, which is below average for this date. The Kogrukluk River weir has a sustainable escapement goal of 13,000-28,000 coho salmon.

Escapement goals are developed using historical run strength data. It is the department’s objective to achieve escapement goals, which ensure sustainable coho salmon runs in the future. The Kuskokwim River amount necessary for subsistence (ANS), as determined by the Board of Fisheries and the public process, is 27,400-57,600 coho salmon. It is unlikely that harvest will meet ANS this year. Given the below average coho salmon passage at the Kuskokwim River sonar, it is warranted to take action to reduce subsistence harvest of coho salmon to achieve the established escapement goal.

The Kuskokwim River sonar will continue operating through the end of August and the Kogrukluk River weir will operate through mid-September. ADF&G will continue to evaluate the coho salmon run and seek consultation from the Kuskokwim River Salmon Management Working Group. Subsistence fishers should stand by for further announcements as the coho salmon run develops. If abundances increase to levels likely to achieve escapement goals, then restrictions to subsistence harvest opportunities may be liberalized.

1827718207.text:
Forrest Bowers, Acting Director

Released: August 18, 2026

Juneau, AK 99811-5526

CONTACT: Matt Olson, Area Management Biologist Bonnie Borba, Fall Season Research Biologist 1-907-459-7274 (Fairbanks) 1-907-949-1320 (Emmonak) Toll free fishing schedule and counts: 1-866-479-7387

2026 Yukon River Salmon Fall Fishery Announcement #12 Fall Update #5, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery Districts Affected: Yukon Area

Inseason assessment suggests the fall chum salmon run size is near the upper end of the drainagewide escapement goal of 300,000–600,000 fish. However, even with a run size near the upper end of the escapement goal range, due to the recently poor proportion of Canadian origin chum returning, Canadian treaty goals may not be met. The interim management escapement goal for the mainstem Yukon River is 70,000–104,000 fall chum salmon and the Fishing Branch River is 22,000–49,000 fall chum salmon. The passage at the Yukon River mainstem sonar project at Pilot Station would likely need to exceed the upper end of the drainagewide escapement goal for fall chum salmon to meet the lower end of the Canadian treaty obligations. Therefore, directed subsistence fishing for fall chum salmon in the mainstem Yukon River is highly unlikely this season in order to protect the Canadian stocks migrating the spawning grounds.

Coho salmon typically enter the Yukon River in mid-August with the bulk of the run passing the Lower Yukon Test Fishery (LYTF) between August 16 and 27. The primary parent year for coho salmon this year is from 2022, which had an estimated index of escapement of 100,000 fish. The run size this year is expected to be well below the average of 212,000 coho salmon. It is still early in the coho salmon run, but current passage estimates are well below average and the run timing appears later than average.

Subsistence fishing for chum and coho salmon was restricted at the start of fall season in each area and nonsalmon subsistence fishing time with 4-inch gillnets is reduced to protect migrating salmon. Assessment projects will continue to monitor the run throughout the migration to determine if there is enough improvement to allow increased fishing opportunity. Assessment project and management updates will be published in weekly Advisory Announcements (Updates). To subscribe to these updates, fill out the form on the following website: https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=cfnews.search

Daily sonar passage estimates and LYTF test fish numbers are shared on Facebook (Yukon River Fishing - ADFG) and can be heard by calling toll-free phone recording: 1-866-479-7387.

Weekly teleconferences hosted by YRDFA take place on Tuesdays at 1:00 p.m. The call-in number is 1800-315-6338, and the participation code is YUKON# (98566#).

Fall Update #5, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery

August 18, 2026

Assessment Projects Lower Yukon Test Fishery (LYTF)/YDFDA and ADF&G

Fall season operations began on July 16 using 6-inch mesh gear to target fall chum and coho salmon. As of August 16, the cumulative CPUE for fall chum salmon was 803.45, which is near the historic cumulative CPUE of 833.74 for this date. The third-quarter point based on median run timing occurs on August 18 for fall season chum salmon at this project. As of August 16, the cumulative CPUE for coho salmon was 5.13, which is well below the historic cumulative CPUE of 118.80 for this date. Fall chum and coho salmon are sampled for ASL (Age, Sex, and Length) and all retained fish are distributed to local communities.

Pilot Station Sonar (ADF&G)

The sonar project operated near Pilot Station transitioned to fall season counts on July 19. As of August 16, the cumulative passage is approximately 445,788 chum salmon in the fall season. This is above the median cumulative passage of 386,000 chum salmon in the fall season for this date. The estimate number of fall chum salmon is 368,439 based on genetic mixed stock analysis. The three-quarter point for fall chum salmon, based on median run timing, occurs on August 22. As of August 16, the cumulative passage is approximately 13,244 coho salmon, which is well below the historic cumulative passage of 36,000 coho salmon for this date. The midpoint for coho salmon based on median run timing occurs on August 22.

Teedriinjik (Chandalar) Sonar / USFWS

This sonar project began operations August 14. As of August 16, the cumulative passage was 276 fall chum salmon, and the daily passage is well below average for this date. The first-quarter point for fall chum salmon based on median timing is September 7, at this project.

Sheenjek River Sonar / ADF&G

This sonar project began operations August 6. As of August 16, the cumulative passage was 406 fall chum salmon, which is below the median of 965 fish. The first-quarter point for fall chum salmon based on median timing is September 8, at this project.

Eagle Sonar / ADF&G and Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO)

This project typically transitions from counting Chinook to fall chum salmon around August 20.

Porcupine River Sonar / Yukon Territory Canada / DFO

This project typically transitions from counting Chinook to fall chum salmon in mid-August.

Fishing Branch River Weir/Sonar / Yukon Territory Canada / DFO

This project will begin counting fall chum salmon sometime in late August to early September.

Fall Age, Sex, and Length Composition

The age composition of 402 chum salmon sampled from the drift gillnets in the LYTF project from July 18 through August 15, consisted of 92% age-4 and 8% age-5 fish. The age-4 fish are well above the 2001– 2025 historical average of 64% age-4. The percentage of female chum salmon has remained low at 41%, which is below the 2001–2025 historical average of 55%. The fall season chum salmon average length through August 15 was 568 mm which is below the 2001–2025 historical average of 583 mm.

Fall Update #5, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery

August 18, 2026

Stock Identification

Genetic mixed stock analysis on chum salmon that passed the mainstem sonar from August 3 through August 10 indicated 5% were summer chum and 95% were fall chum salmon. Of the fall chum salmon stocks they consisted of 55% Border US (Teedriinjik, Sheenjek, Draanjik and Coleen), 36% Tanana fall, and 9% Canada. For fall chum salmon this represents 91% U.S.-origin and 9% Canada-origin stocks. The fall chum salmon Border US and Tanana fall components are above average while the Canadian stock is below average for this time period. The results are provided in the ADF&G Yukon River daily update for those who subscribe: https://list.state.ak.us/mailman/listinfo/yukonriverdailyupdate

Summer Assessment Projects

Chena River Tower (ADF&G)

Tower operations ended August 14. Chinook salmon passage was estimated to be 1,546 fish which is below the historical cumulative average of 4,711 fish. Summer chum salmon cumulative passage is estimated to be 5,876 fish which is below the historical cumulative median of 6,883 fish. Chum salmon passage rates remained high at the end of the project and passage should be considered a minimum estimate.

Salcha River Tower (ADF&G)

Tower operations ended August 16. Chinook salmon passage was estimated to be 1,976 fish, which is below the historical cumulative average of 7,092 fish. Summer chum salmon cumulative passage is estimated to be 13,216 fish which is below the historical cumulative median of 17,289 fish. Only a few tower counts were affected by high water but passage estimates for chum salmon should be considered a minimum estimate as the project ended before the run was complete.

Chinook Radio Telemetry (ADF&G)

2026 is the start of the second phase of a multi-year effort to evaluate concerns for Chinook en route mortality and spawning distribution within Canada. This is the first year of an up to three-year effort to capture and tag up to 250 Chinook salmon each season near Rampart Rapids. Tagged fish will be tracked throughout the upper Yukon in Alaska and Canada to evaluate en-route mortality and spawning distribution. Tagging at Rapids concluded on July 28, but tracking operations are ongoing using remote tracking towers and aerial surveys within both Alaska and Canada. Each fish was tagged with both an internal radio telemetry tag and an external spaghetti tag. If you encounter a tagged fish this season and are successful at documenting the tag number, please call 1-877-467-2104 to report information about when and where the fish was observed. As a thank you for voluntarily reporting the tag number and associated information, you will be automatically entered into the ADF&G salmon tag lottery at the Fred West at 907-267-2237 with any questions.

Eagle Sonar (ADF&G)

Sonar operations began on June 30. As of August 17, Chinook salmon passage is estimated to be 34,289 ± 378 fish (90% confidence interval), which is below the historical cumulative average of 46,959 fish. Assuming normal run timing, the Chinook salmon run is over 99% complete at the U.S./Canada border. The cumulative passage of Chinook salmon at Eagle sonar is below average and will not meet the international border passage objective, but the estimate is larger than what has been observed since 2020. The average transition date between counting Chinook and fall chum salmon at this project is August 18

Current Subsistence Management Actions

Fishing for nonsalmon remains open, but it is limited to non-lethal or selective gear types including hook and line with a rod or pole, dip net, beach seine, hand line, longline, and fyke net.

Coastal District, District 1, District 2, District 3, District 4, Subdistrict 4-A Upper, Subdistrict 4-B, Subdistrict 4-C, Subdistrict 5-A, Subdistrict 5-B, Subdistrict 5-C, Subdistrict 5-D Lower, Subdistrict 5-D Middle, Subdistrict 5-D Upper, Subdistrict 6-A, Subdistrict 6-B, and the Porcupine River (from the Naskonat Peninsula, north to Point Romanof, upstream to the U.S./Canada border, and from the mouth of the Tanana River upstream to the Wood River, including the Kantishna River Drainage, snd the communities of Chevak, Hooper Bay, Scammon Bay, Emmonak, Nunam Iqua, Alakanuk, Kotlik, Mountain Village, Pitkas Point, St. Mary’s, Pilot Station, Marshall, Russian Mission, Holy Cross, Grayling, Anvik, Kaltag, Nulato, Koyukuk, Galena, Ruby, Tanana, Rampart, Stevens Village, Beaver, Venetie, Chalkyitsik, Birch Creek, Fort Yukon, Circle, Eagle, Lake Minchumina, Manley, Minto, and Nenana):

Subsistence fishing for Chinook, chum, and coho salmon is closed and these salmon species must be released alive. Fishing for nonsalmon remains open 24 hours a day, seven days per week with nonlethal or selective gear types including manned fish wheels, hook and line with a rod or pole, dip net, beach seine, hand line, longline, and fyke net. Fall Update #5, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery

Gillnets of 4-inch or smaller mesh may be used to target nonsalmon from noon Thursdays, through noon Sundays. Nets are restricted to 60-feet or less in length and must be operated as a set net near shore.

6-inch or Smaller Mesh Gillnet Nonsalmon Opportunity in Designated Areas

Subsistence fishing for whitefish and other nonsalmon species with 6-inch or smaller mesh set gillnets is open only in designated nonsalmon areas 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. Set gillnets are restricted 60-feet or shorter in length and cannot block more than ½ width of any waterway. Please see Fall Season Advisory Announcements #1-#4, #7, and #9 for the named lists, GPS coordinates, and maps of these designated areas. Links to Advisory Announcements and maps are shared on the ADFG – Yukon River Fishing Facebook page.

In Lake Minchumina and the Tolovana River drainage, including Minto Flats, subsistence fishing for nonsalmon will remain open 24 hours a day, seven days per week with 6-inch or smaller mesh gillnets.

A subsistence fishing permit is required for all species in the portion of Subdistrict 5-C from the westernmost tip of Garnet Island upstream to the ADF&G regulatory marker two miles downstream of Waldron Creek (Dalton Highway bridge area) and in Subdistricts 6-A and 6-B including the Kantishna River drainage and for northern pike in the Tolovana River drainage, including Minto Flats.

Koyukuk River drainage upstream of a line from 64° 53.273' N, 157° 40.760' W, to 64° 53.020' N, 157° 39.887' W (including the communities of Huslia, Hughes, Allakaket, Alatna, Bettles, and Wiseman)

Subsistence fishing for salmon and nonsalmon is open 24 hours per day, 7 days per week with 6-inch or smaller mesh gillnets and all other legal subsistence fishing gear. All fish caught may be retained. Please see Fall Season Advisory Announcements #11 for the GPS coordinates and map of this area.

A subsistence fishing permit is also required for all species in the Koyukuk River above Bettles including the community of Wiseman. Gillnet gear in this permit area must be 3½ inches or smaller mesh size and cannot be used until August 20.

Innoko River drainage upstream of a line from 62° 11.241' N, 159° 39.397' W, to 62° 11.121' N, 159° 39.227' W and Paimiut Slough upstream of a line from 61° 55.989' N, 160° 08.985' W, to 61° 55.986' N, 160° 08.717' W (including the community of Shageluk):

Subsistence fishing for salmon and nonsalmon is open 24 hours per day, 7 days per week with 6-inch or smaller mesh gillnets and all other legal subsistence fishing gear. All fish caught may be retained. Please see Fall Season Advisory Announcements #11 for the GPS coordinates and maps of these areas.

Upper Tanana Area (the Tanana River from the confluence with the mouth of Volkmar River on the north bank and the mouth of the Johnson River on the south bank upstream to the Tanana River headwaters, including Delta Junction area, Dot Lake, Tanacross, Tetlin, Tok, Northway, and Nabesna):

Chinook, chum, and coho salmon fishing is closed. Fish wheels and gillnets with larger than 4-inch mesh and fish wheels are not allowed. Gillnets of 4-inch or smaller mesh may be used to target other species and are restricted to 60-feet or less in length and must be operated as a set net near shore. Chinook, chum, and coho salmon must be released alive immediately from selective gear types.

Fall Update #5, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery

August 18, 2026

Fishermen are reminded that a subsistence permit is required to fish for salmon in the Tanana River drainage up to the Wood River (Subdistrict 6-A, 6-B, and Kantishna River drainage), northern pike in the Tolovana River drainage (including Minto Flats), and all species in the Upper Tanana Area. A subsistence salmon permit is not required in Lake Minchumina.

Personal Use Management Actions

Subdistrict 6-C (Personal use fishery from the regulatory marker at the mouth of the Wood River upstream to the downstream mouth of the Salcha River, which includes the communities of Fairbanks, North Pole, and Salcha):

Personal Use salmon fishing is closed until further notice.

Personal Use Whitefish and Sucker Fishing

Fairbanks Nonsubsistence Area (a portion of the Tanana River drainage from the Wood River upstream to the mouth of the Volkmar River on the north bank and the mouth of the Johnson River on the south bank, which includes Fairbanks, North Pole, Salcha, and Delta Junction):

Personal Use whitefish and sucker fishing with manned fishwheels is closed until further notice. Fishing with other gear for whitefish and suckers in this area remains open 7 days per week, 24 hours per day, subject to permit stipulations.

A reminder to personal use fishermen that a personal use salmon permit is required to fish for salmon in Subdistrict 6-C and a personal use whitefish and sucker permit is required to fish for these species in the Fairbanks Nonsubsistence Area. Both permits require a valid sport fishing license.

Federal Special Action

The Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) have coordinated on this advisory announcement. The USFWS Federal Inseason Manager has issued separate Fishery special actions with the same fishing restrictions and schedule in waters adjacent to Federal Land. In Federal public waters, the salmon subsistence fishing opportunity is limited to federally qualified subsistence users in the Yukon River drainage. For additional information concerning Yukon River Federal Special Actions contact the USFWS Federal Yukon River Subsistence Fishery Manager, Holly Carroll; holly_carroll@fws.gov, (907) 351-3029 or Assistant Manager, Keith Herron; keith_herron@fws.gov, (907) 334-5391.

This is an announcement by the ADF&G in cooperation with the USFWS.

Federal Special Actions will be posted on www.doi.gov/subsistence/fisheries-special-actions and shared on Facebook at www.facebook.com/subsistencealaska.

SOUTHEAST ALASKA/YAKUTAT SUMMER TROLL FISHERY ANNOUNCEMENT

The Southeast Alaska/Yakutat commercial troll fishery will close to the taking of all salmon at 11:59 p.m., August 8, 2026, except within the hatchery chum salmon and terminal harvest areas (THA) noted below. The fishery will be closed for 4 days, from August 9 through 12, 2026, and will reopen to the taking of all salmon at 12:01 a.m., August 13, 2026.

Chinook Salmon Retention Period The troll fishery will open for the retention of Chinook salmon at 12:01 a.m., August 13, 2026, and will remain open until closed by emergency order. An estimated 82,000 treaty Chinook salmon will be harvested by trollers during the first summer opening, leaving approximately 36,000 Chinook salmon (including a 2% Alaska hatchery component) to harvest during the second opening. Beginning 12:01 a.m., August 13, the areas of high Chinook salmon abundance will open by emergency order until further notice (5 AAC 29.100[c][2][A]). The retention period will be managed inseason with no predetermined length and will be closed by emergency order.

Trollers are strongly encouraged to contact the troll fishery managers during the retention period to report harvest and effort information via phone (747-6688; voicemail available after hours, dial * and extension 237) or email (grant.hagerman@alaska.gov or isabel.platten@alaska.gov). The fishery closure will be announced by ADF&G advisory announcement, will be recorded on the ADF&G troll fishery telephone hotline, and may be broadcasted over the United States Coast Guard and National Weather Service marine broadcasts.

Reporting and Landing Requirements Following the closure of the Chinook and coho salmon fishery, all Chinook and coho salmon must be offloaded from a vessel prior to participating in the hatchery chum salmon fisheries described below. Fish tickets must be submitted to the department within 7 days of landing. A catcher–processor (FAS) that does not participate in the chum fishery during the troll closure is not required to offload their frozen product.

A catcher–processor (FAS) that retains frozen Chinook or coho salmon onboard through the closure and into the next Chinook salmon opening must submit a fish ticket to the department within seven days after offloading those Chinook and coho salmon.

Hatchery Chum Salmon Fishery Trollers may target chum salmon during the troll closure, August 9–12, 2026, in the areas described below. Chum, pink, and sockeye salmon may be retained; however, coho and Chinook salmon may not be retained during these fisheries (5 AAC 29.112).

Neets Bay (101-90): waters of Neets Bay east of the longitude of Chin Point at 131°42.10′ W long, and west of the longitude of the easternmost tip of Bug Island at 131°39.14′ W long (Figure 1).

West Crawfish Inlet (113-32): waters of West Crawfish Inlet and Windy Passage, southeast of a line from 56°47.11′ N lat, 135°18.87′ W long, to 56°46.89′ N lat, 135°19.92′ W long, northeast of a line from 56°45.80′ N lat, 135°20.06′ W long, to 56°45.30′ N lat, 135°17.64′ W long, and northwest of a line from 56°45.32′ N lat, 135°16.99′ W long, to 56°45.36′ N lat, 135°16.89′ W long, in First Narrows (Figure 2).

Crawfish Inlet THA (113-33): waters south of 56°47.14′ N lat in Cedar Pass, northeast of a line from 56°43.83′ N lat, 135°16.13′ W long to 56°43.49′ N lat, 135°15.50′ W long in Middle Channel, and north of a line from 56°43.01′ N lat, 135°12.93′ W long to 56°43.25′ N lat, 135°12.18′ W long in Walker Channel. The waters of Bear Cove will remain closed (Figure 3).

Terminal Harvest Areas During the closure period, trolling will remain open to all species in the Herring Bay Troll THA (101-40) and the Anita Bay THA (107-35). Chinook and coho salmon harvested in THAs listed above must be offloaded prior to trolling outside THA boundaries in the hatchery chum salmon fisheries during the troll closure period.

2026 NEETS BAY TERMINAL HARVEST AREA FISHERIES ANNOUNCEMENT

The Southern Southeast Regional Aquaculture Association (SSRAA) has achieved their cost recovery goal and secured summer chum salmon broodstock. The Neets Bay Terminal Harvest Area (THA) will open for rotational fisheries beginning at 5:00 a.m., Thursday, August 6, 2026.

SOUTHEAST ALASKA/YAKUTAT SUMMER TROLL FISHERY UPDATE

The first Chinook salmon retention period of the general summer commercial troll season will remain open until further notice. Based on landed catch and reported harvest onboard freezer vessels to date, less than 40,000 of the 83,700 Chinook salmon allocation has been harvested over the first 10-days of the fishery. The department will continue to closely monitor the fishery and will announce any forthcoming closure via emergency order when we approach the harvest target.

Trollers are strongly encouraged to contact the troll fishery managers at the Sitka Area Office during the retention period to report catch and effort information via phone (747-6688; voicemail available after hours, dial * and extension 237) or email (grant.hagerman@alaska.gov or isabel.platten@alaska.gov). The fishery closure will be announced by Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) advisory announcement and troll fishery telephone hotline. Closure announcements will be submitted for broadcast on the United States Coast Guard and National Weather Service marine information broadcasts. The Summer Troll Fishery Management Plan is available at ADF&G area offices and the troll website at:

CATCHER–PROCESSOR VESSELS

Catcher–processors intending to freeze their catch onboard (FAS) during the summer troll fishery must obtain a 2026 Summer Troll Fishery Exemption Permit from the department to legally remove the heads from adipose-fin-clipped salmon (5 AAC 29.140[b] and 5 AAC 29.145[c]). The permit, available at area offices and on the troll fishery website, is not valid until signed by a department representative.

Catcher–processors are required to complete and submit a separate fish ticket for each week (Sunday through Saturday) and are encouraged to contact the troll managers periodically with catch information.

LANDING AND REPORTING REQUIREMENTS

Fish tickets for the summer troll fishery must include a record of the 5-digit statistical area and a description of the nearest headland or bay in which the fish were taken (5 AAC 39.130[c][8]). DEEP INLET TERMINAL HARVEST AREA FISHERIES ANNOUNCEMENT

The following information details the Northern Southeast Regional Aquaculture Association (NSRAA) Deep Inlet Terminal Harvest Area (THA) common property fisheries open waters and fishing schedules for the 2026 season.

The Deep Inlet THA is scheduled to open on June 1, 2026. NSRAA is projecting a total run of 13,900 Chinook, 37,000 coho, and 1,763,000 chum salmon for the Medvejie Hatchery and Deep Inlet THA in 2026. NSRAA will be conducting cost-recovery operations in the Deep Inlet THA beginning June 28. To accommodate cost-recovery operations, the entire Deep Inlet THA will be closed to all common property commercial harvest from June 28 until cost-recovery operations are completed.

Unless modified by subsequent advisory announcement, salmon may be taken in the Deep Inlet THA from Monday, June 1 through Saturday, June 27, 2026, as follows:

Purse Seine

• From June 1 through June 27, the purse seine fishery will be open from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., Sunday,

Thursday, and Friday of each week.

Drift Gillnet

• From June 1 through June 27, the drift gillnet fishery will be open from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., Monday,

Tuesday, and Wednesday of each week.

Troll

• From June 1 through June 27, the troll fishery will be open from 12:01 a.m. to 11:59 p.m., Saturday of each

week and during those periods the net fisheries are closed.

• Additionally, From June 1 through June 20 only, the troll fishery will be open continuously within the

boundaries of the Deep Inlet THA west of 135°20.75′ W long.

Trollers are reminded that all fish retained within the boundaries of the Deep Inlet THA listed below must be reported as being harvested in statistical area 113-38.

The Deep Inlet THA is described as follows:

Deep Inlet THA: will be closed west of 135°20.75′ W long to purse seine and drift gillnet gear from June 1 through June 20.

Deep Inlet THA salmon streams: no restrictions will be in effect for Deep Inlet THA salmon streams (all freshwaters and stream channels remain closed).

Drift gillnets are restricted to a minimum mesh size of 6 inches through June 20 to reduce the harvest of wild sockeye salmon returning to Silver Bay.

By emergency order issued under 5 AAC 39.265, harvesters participating in purse seine and drift gillnet fisheries in the Deep Inlet THA are required to retain all salmon harvested.

Fishermen, tenders, and processors are reminded that all salmon, including steelhead, commercially harvested but retained for personal use and not sold, must be reported on fish tickets at the time of delivery.

Fishermen are advised that if they have fish on board from other fishing areas outside of the Deep Inlet THA, they should keep them separate for reporting and sampling purposes.

Chinook Salmon Landing Restrictions for the Deep Inlet THA: Purse seine and drift gillnet fishermen must retain all Chinook salmon harvested in the Deep Inlet THA. Chinook salmon of any size harvested by both purse seine and drift gillnet fishermen may be sold. Troll fishermen may only retain and sell Chinook salmon greater than 28 inches.

To reduce conflicts with private landowners, NSRAA is requesting that all fishing vessels and tenders not anchor, use highintensity lights, or tender fish near Berry Island within the Deep Inlet THA; additionally, NSRAA requests that vessels use no-wake speeds when entering Deep Inlet via Silver Point. Additional information and a chart of preferred anchorage areas is available from the NSRAA office or online at https://www.nsraa.org/.

The Crawfish Inlet Terminal Harvest Area (THA) salmon troll fishery will be open for the harvest of salmon from 12:01 a.m., Monday, June 1, through 11:59 p.m., Sunday, September 20, 2026, unless closed by emergency order.

The Crawfish Inlet THA (statistical area 113-33) consists of the waters east of a line from 56°44.21′ N lat, 135°15.76′ W long, to 56°43.30′ N lat, 135°17.80′ W long, to 56°41.93′ N lat, 135°17.54′ W long, to 56°41.14′ N lat, 135°13.80′ W long, including the waters of Jamboree Bay and Cedar Pass south of 56°47.14′ N lat, and Crawfish Inlet west of 135°11.05′ W long (Figure 1). Troll fishery participants are advised that the bolded coordinates have been modified by emergency order to position the location of the THA boundary point on the shoreline of Lodge Island.

Chinook salmon Chinook salmon retention is permitted in the Crawfish Inlet THA during the spring troll fishery from June 1 through June 30. Other salmon Coho, chum, pink, and sockeye salmon retention is permitted during open fishing periods from June 1 through September 20. The troll fishery will remain open continuously in the troll exclusive area outside the waters of the Crawfish Inlet SHA from June 1 through September 20, unless closed by emergency order.

THOMAS BAY TERMINAL HARVEST AREA FISHERIES ANNOUNCEMENT

The following information details the Northern Southeast Alaska Regional Aquaculture Association (NSRAA) commercial fishing open waters and fishing schedules in the Thomas Bay Terminal Harvest Area (THA) for the 2026 season.

NSRAA is forecasting a total run of 115,000 chum salmon to Thomas Bay THA (Figure 1). This year’s run will be the 8th for this project and will be comprised of all age classes. A portion of the run may be harvested in common property fisheries in Chatham Strait and Frederick Sound.

The Thomas Bay THA are those waters of Thomas Bay northeast of a line from Point Vandeput at 57°00.96′ N lat, 133°00.02′ W long, to Wood Point at 56°59.55′ N lat, 132°56.96′ W long, northwest of a line from a point on the mainland shoreline at 56°59.57′ N lat, 132°54.02′ W long to Ruth Island at 57°00.42′ N lat, 132°51.07′ W long, north of line from a point on the southeastern shoreline of Ruth Island at 56°58.70′ N lat, 132°49.16′ W long, to the mainland shoreline at 56°58.70′ N lat, 132°47.32′ W long, west of a line from the mainland shoreline at 56°59.38′ N lat, 132°47.60′ W long, to the southern tip of Spray Island at 56°59.80′ N lat, 132°47.73′ W long, to the northern tip of Spray Island at 57°00.07′ N lat, 132°47.80′ W long, to the mainland shoreline at 57°00.56′ N lat, 132°47.57′ W long, and south of a line from 57°03.00′ N lat, 132°49.62′ W long, to 57°03.00′ N lat, 132°52.03′ W long, with the following restrictions:

Spurt Cove: waters of Spurt Cove are closed northwest of a line from 57°01.98′ N lat, 132°52.49′ W long, to 57°02.08′ N lat, 132°52.37′ W long;

Thomas Bay Bluffs: waters northeast of a line from the northern tip of Spray Island at 57°00.07′ N lat, 132°47.80′ W long to a point on the northern boundary line approximately 0.5 nautical mile from the mainland shoreline at 57°03.00′ N lat, 132°50.55′ W long, are closed every Saturday and Sunday of each week from 12:01 a.m., Saturday, to 11:59 p.m., Sunday.

Purse seine: will be open from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., Sunday and Thursday each week, from Sunday, June 21, through Thursday, August 6, 2026.

Troll: will be open during those periods the purse seine fishery is closed from 12:01 a.m., Sunday, June 21, through 11:59 p.m., Saturday, August 8, 2026.

Chinook Salmon Landing Restrictions for Thomas Bay THA: Chinook salmon retention is permitted in the troll fishery only during general summer troll Chinook salmon retention periods established under 5 AAC 29.100; trollers may retain and sell only those Chinook salmon that are 28 inches or greater in length. Chinook salmon caught in the purse seine fishery 28 inches or greater in length may only be retained during retention periods established by emergency order for the Southeast Alaska purse seine fishery, and Chinook salmon less than 28 inches may be retained but not sold.
